library(broom)
load("../data/Cleaned_Pilot/EDA.RData") 
Neuroethics_Judgement %>% 
  select(user_id, Risk_Beta, Gain_Beta, age, Income, republican, democrat, independent, 
conservative, liberal, Political_Party, ReligionRaised, ReligionNow, Religiosity, Spirituality, 
AttendChurch, ReligiousActivity, meditation, Harm, Fairness, Loyalty, Athority, Sancticy) %>% 
  distinct() %>% 
  mutate(log.risk = log1p(abs(min(Risk_Beta)) + Risk_Beta)) %>% 
  mutate(log.gain = log1p(abs(min(Gain_Beta)) + Gain_Beta)) %>% 
  filter(!user_id == "tTZWd9tg") %>% 
  filter(!user_id == "ZJ8tICU0") %>% 
  filter(!user_id == "FIvIqXVg") -> data 
data$republican <- factor(data$republican,
                     ordered = TRUE,
                     levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7"))
data$democrat <- factor(data$democrat,
                     ordered = TRUE,
                     levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7"))
data$independent <- factor(data$independent,
                     ordered = TRUE,
                     levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7"))
data$conservative <- factor(data$conservative,
                     ordered = TRUE,
                     levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7"))
data$liberal <- factor(data$liberal,
                     ordered = TRUE,
                     levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7"))
data$Income <-as.character(data$Income) 
data$Income <- str_remove(data$Income, "[>,]")
data$Income<- str_trim(data$Income)
data$Income <- as.numeric(data$Income)
####################
ggplot(data, aes(log.risk)) + geom_density()

ggplot(data, aes(log.gain)) + geom_density()

ggplot(data, aes(age,log.risk)) + geom_point() 

ggplot(data, aes(age,log.gain)) + geom_point() 

ggplot(data, aes(Income,log.risk)) + geom_point() 

ggplot(data, aes(Income,log.gain)) + geom_point() 

#Republican
ggplot(data, aes(republican, log.risk, fill= republican)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data, aes(republican, log.gain, fill= republican)) + geom_boxplot()

#Democrat
ggplot(data, aes(democrat, log.risk, fill= democrat)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data, aes(democrat, log.gain, fill= democrat)) + geom_boxplot()

#independent
ggplot(data, aes(independent, log.risk, fill= independent)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data, aes(independent, log.gain, fill= independent)) + geom_boxplot()

#conservative
ggplot(data, aes(conservative, log.risk, fill= conservative)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data, aes(conservative, log.gain, fill= conservative)) + geom_boxplot()

#liberal
ggplot(data, aes(liberal, log.risk, fill= liberal)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data, aes(liberal, log.gain, fill= liberal)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data, aes(Political_Party,log.risk, fill = Political_Party)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data, aes(Political_Party,log.gain, fill = Political_Party)) + geom_boxplot()

Prior studies suggest that medical ethical judgments can be influenced by a person’s political ideology and religious values.

We predict liberals and democrats will be, on average, less sensitive to risks of harm, and more sensitive to benefits,

Testing for means differences between dems and reps

data %>% 
  select(user_id, Political_Party, log.risk, log.gain) -> subset
subset <- subset(subset, Political_Party != "Independent")
subset <- subset(subset, Political_Party != "Other")
# Sort by beta type then user_id so that the t test function reads it
subset <- subset[order(subset$Political_Party, subset$user_id), ]
# Welch t-test
#tests differences between rep and dems on each of our responses
t1 <- t.test(log.risk ~ Political_Party, subset, var.equal=TRUE)
t2 <- t.test(log.gain ~ Political_Party, subset, var.equal=TRUE)
#create table
tab <- map_df(list(t1, t2), tidy)
knitr::kable(tab[c("method","estimate", "statistic", "conf.low", "conf.high", "p.value")])
method estimate statistic conf.low conf.high p.value

Aim 2) To explore the relationship between existing moral intuitions and judgments about abstract technologies involving a risk of harm and likelihood of gain.

Consistent with MFT we hypothesize that higher scores on foundations of Authority, Loyalty, and Sanctity will be more risk averse than those who score high on Harm and Fairness.

Winsorization began as a way to "robustify" the sample mean, which is sensitive to extreme values. To obtain the Winsorized mean, you sort the data and replace the smallest k values by the (k+1)st smallest value. You do the same for the largest values, replacing the k largest values with the (k+1)st largest value. The mean of this new set of numbers is called the Winsorized mean. If the data are from a symmetric population, the Winsorized mean is a robust unbiased estimate of the population mean.
